item.title: Fires Char New Guinea
item.summary: Emissions on both sides of the island are unusually high as human-set fires spread in a landscape parched by drought.
item.page_text:
Emissions on both sides of the island are unusually high as human-set fires spread in a landscape parched by drought.
New Guinea, the world's second-largest island, harbors an extraordinary variety of plant life across more than a dozen distinct ecoregions , including seasonally dry savannas, tropical rainforests, and lowland swamp forests. But in September and October 2026, as drought gripped New Guinea (sometimes called Papua) amid a strong El Niño , fires scorched the island and smoke shrouded large swaths of it for weeks.
The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-20 satellite captured this image of thick smoke streaming from the southern part of the island on October 11, 2026. In recent weeks, soaring levels of air pollution delayed and canceled flights , closed schools, and prompted officials in some areas to urge children and older people to wear masks.
"Sometimes smoke that has drifted into the convection of nearby thunderstorms will get washed out or lofted up into the upper troposphere, but a lot of smoke stays near the surface and causes air quality problems," said Robert Field, an associate research scientist at NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies and Columbia University. "It's a horrible situation."
According to the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED), a fire emissions monitoring system, fires in Papua New Guinea, on the eastern half of the island, had released nearly 32 megatons of carbon by October 19, more than any other year on record at that point in the year. "Emissions are already much higher than the 2015 total for the year, and it's very likely that this will become the highest year on record for Papua New Guinea, even surpassing 1997," said Guido van der Werf, a fire scientist at Wageningen University & Research.
On the Indonesian side, sometimes called West New Guinea or Indonesian Papua, carbon emissions exceeded 35 megatons , the third highest after 2015 and 1997, other El Niño years with severe fires. Van der Werf led the development of GFED, a satellite-driven modeling framework that uses a mix of remote sensing , vegetation characteristics, and other information to estimate the extent of vegetation fires and the emissions over nearly three decades.
Unusually dry weather—a byproduct of El Niño shifting rainfall patterns —has primed ecosystems across the island to burn. The southernmost part of Papua New Guinea, dominated by relatively fire-prone savannas and grasslands of the Trans-Fly region , went more than 90 consecutive days without rain, according to Papua New Guinea's National Weather Service . Since August, parts of the region have seen precipitation of roughly 5 to 10 percent of normal, according to the weather service's data. Local news outlets report that drought is causing crop failures , water shortages , and school disruptions .
In this normally wet part of the world, people ignite the vast majority of fires, researchers say. Crop fires, pasture maintenance, deforestation and land clearing, and hunting are all common reasons people burn in New Guinea. In dry conditions, managed fires sometimes spread and burn uncontrolled as wildfires, particularly in the drier, southernmost parts of the island.
"We're seeing an exceptionally high level of fire activity in Papua New Guinea and Eastern Indonesia, particularly Indonesian Papua and Kalimantan, this year compared with Sumatra and other parts of Western Indonesia," said Yang Chen, an associate researcher at the University of California, Irvine. "Papua has emerged as Indonesia’s new deforestation frontier."
Over the past two decades , land in Indonesian Papua has been cleared for industrial oil palm and pulpwood plantations, shifting small-scale cultivation, urban expansion, and mining . According to Global Forest Watch, the region lost 27,000 hectares of primary forest in 2025, nearly double the 2024 total and the most since 2017.
Sumatra's fires are relatively low compared to other drought years partly because many areas are already developed. "Areas with large oil palm, sugarcane, or pulpwood plantations also often have their own private fire brigades to protect their assets," said Field. "It's in unmanaged areas or primary forest edges where we're generally seeing the most fire."
Researchers expect the fires to continue until the heavy rains of the wet season arrive in the southern part of New Guinea, typically in early November.
NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE , GIBS/Worldview , and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS). Story by Adam Voiland.

item.page_text:
Do you remember the World's Most Notable    People Map . On Monday, I decided I'd build a World's Most Notable Places Map , showing locations based on their Wikipedia QRank. I abandoned the project today after discovering the Wikipedia Importance Map .
Earlier this month, Wikimedia Enterprise released the Geospatial Wikidata Databset .. This is a large, open dataset that connects geographic features in OpenStreetMap (OSM) with information held in Wikidata, Wikipedia and Wikivoyage.
The idea behind the dataset is simple but powerful: OpenStreetMap tells you where things are and provides their geographic shapes, while Wikimedia projects can tell you what they are, why they matter and what is known about them. The dataset does the hard work of linking these sources together, making it easier to query this information without building your own complicated data-processing pipeline.
My bright idea was to use the Geospatial Wikidata Dataset to create A Map of the World's Most Notable Places , using Wikidata's QRank. QRank is a ranking signal for Wikidata entities, which correspond to subjects represented in Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. It measures their relative popularity across the whole Wikimedia ecosystem.
Which brings us to the Wikipedia Importance Map . The Wikipedia Importance Map maps geolocated Wikipedia articles around the world, with the size of each label reflecting the importance of the subject. The map combines two different measures of importance: PageRank , which analyses how Wikipedia articles link to one another across all language editions, and QRank , which uses pageviews to measure how popular articles are. The result is an interactive map that lets you explore the world through the subjects that attract the most attention on Wikipedia.
Even more interestingly, the map doesn't limit itself to articles with their own geographic coordinates. It also includes around 2.5 million subjects that can be associated with a place, such as people mapped to their birthplace, paintings to their museum, battles to where they were fought, and companies to their headquarters. These are displayed as colored dots, spread around the relevant town or city.
There is also a second map, the Wikivoyage Travel Map , which uses Wikivoyage data to map destinations and travel recommendations. It includes places to see, things to do, shopping, eating, drinking and sleeping, with their size determined by how often travellers read about them.
Exploring the places with the highest QRank in a particular area is an interesting way to discover its most prominent landmarks, people and historical events. It can help you identify places to visit, uncover local stories or simply find out what makes a particular town or city notable.
One caveat: a large label indicates importance according to the map's combined ranking signals, not necessarily historical significance or how worthwhile a place is to visit. It's a discovery tool, rather than a definitive guide to the world's most important places.

NASA has revealed new details about its plans to return astronauts to the surface of the moon, outlining a series of upcoming milestones for SpaceX and Blue Origin as both companies race to ready their lunar landers for the agency's Artemis program .
During an Oct. 5 presentation at the Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Antalya, Türkiye, Steve Creech, acting manager of NASA's Human Landing System (HLS) Program, laid out development timelines for both spacecraft, with key demonstrations planned through early 2028 that include orbital refueling and uncrewed lunar landing tests to qualify the vehicles to fly astronauts to the surface of the moon .
A more pressing deadline, however, is NASA's Artemis III mission, which is targeted for the third quarter (Q3) of 2027. Artemis III will launch four astronauts aboard NASA's Orion spacecraft to low Earth orbit (LEO), where they will rendezvous and dock with test versions of both companies' landers for interoperability checkouts. Those demonstrations will help inform NASA's determination about which lander the agency will choose to carry astronauts to the moon's surface on Artemis IV, targeted for early 2028.
SpaceX and Blue Origin were both awarded NASA contracts to develop HLS vehicles — Starship and Blue Moon , respectively — and have spent the past several years refining their respective lunar lander designs and dealing with various delays along the way. In the face of those delays, and in an effort to better structure its mission progression for success, NASA overhauled its Artemis program architecture in February to maintain its goal of landing astronauts on the moon by the end of 2028 and establish a more regular cadence of uncrewed landings in the meantime.
As part of that shakeup, Artemis III, previously the program's first crewed lunar landing mission, was moved up a year and repurposed for the lunar lander vehicle tests the agency is preparing to fly to LEO next year. The program's first moon landing remains scheduled for 2028, but was shifted to the manifest for Artemis IV.
Between now and then, both SpaceX and Blue Origin have more than a dozen test demonstrations and vehicle milestones to achieve, including success during Artemis III and flights afterward. This will all lead up to a key decision NASA must make: Which vehicle will carry out the first crewed landing on the surface of the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972?
Starship reached for the first time on its most recent test flight, which occurred on Sept. 28 from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. NASA lists several other important goals for the vehicle to achieve in 2026, including (in the order listed during the IAC presentation) the first return and catch of the rocket's upgraded Version 3 (V3) booster at its launch pad; the first-ever return and catch of a Ship upper stage; the first Starship launch from one of SpaceX's launch pads still under construction on Florida's Space Coast; and, possibly, the first V3 booster reflight.
NASA also expects SpaceX to complete the initial build of the crew cabin for its lunar lander Starship variant. SpaceX released renders of Starship's interior last year , as well as images of the test elevator astronauts are using to train for Starship egress on the lunar surface, but little else has been made public about the progress the company has made on the cabin's design.
Should the cabin's initial build wrap up by the end of the year, as NASA's presentation suggested, SpaceX will use Q1 2027 to complete integration of the systems that Starship will need to communicate with Orion during Artemis III, and deliver a cabin simulator for astronauts to train on leading up to the mission. SpaceX plans to continue Starship test flights through Q2 of next year, complete a landing leg demonstration and begin crew cabin airlock tests.
Blue Origin's lunar lander mockup is ready for NASA Artemis astronaut training
For Artemis III, SpaceX plans to fly one of its existing V3 Starship upper stages, with some slight modifications. Starship and Orion will dock as part of Artemis III but the SpaceX vehicle won't be equipped with a crew cabin for the mission's astronauts to enter. Between the end of this year and the beginning of the next, SpaceX is expected to complete the addition of a docking system and nosecone cover to the Artemis III Starship vehicle, which, NASA documents suggest, has already completed its mechanical fit checks.

item.title: Mapped: The Cost of Raising a Child in Every U.S. State
item.summary: Explore the cost of raising a child by state, from over $412,000 in Hawaii to about $202,000 in New Hampshire.
item.page_text:
Raising a child to age 18 costs an estimated $303,418 nationwide, but the total can vary by more than $210,000 depending on where a family lives.
Much of that difference comes down to housing, transportation, and childcare expenses, which can significantly affect the cost of raising a child from one state to another.
This visualization uses a 2026 study from LendingTree to compare the projected cost of raising a child across all 50 states and Washington, D.C.
Hawaii is the most expensive state by a considerable margin, with an estimated 18-year cost of $412,661. That’s nearly $48,000 more than second-place Alaska ($365,047) and over $86,000 more than Maryland ($326,360), which ranks third.
California and New Jersey round out the top five, both at approximately $312,000.
Perhaps the biggest surprise is Kansas, which ranks sixth at $303,250. Despite its reputation for affordability, the state has a higher projected child-rearing cost than New York, Massachusetts, and Washington.
The table below shows the estimated cost of raising a child to age 18 in every state and Washington, D.C.
At the other end of the ranking, New Hampshire has the lowest projected cost at $201,963, followed by Washington, D.C. ($202,115) and South Carolina ($204,213).
Costs also vary considerably within states. San Francisco, for example, has an estimated annual child-rearing cost of $43,171, the highest among 48 major metropolitan areas in our ranking of the most expensive U.S. cities to raise a child .
LendingTree’s estimates include additional expenses associated with having a child, such as food, rent, daycare, clothing, transportation, and health insurance premiums. The calculations account for state tax exemptions and credits but exclude the federal child tax credit and college expenses.
Alaska ranks as the second-most expensive state to raise a child, but childcare isn’t the main reason.
According to LendingTree, Alaska has the highest additional rent and transportation expenses associated with raising a child. These costs help push its projected 18-year total to $365,047.
Interestingly, annual infant daycare costs approximately $12,100 in Alaska, well below the national figure of roughly $17,000.
The first five years of raising a child can cost more than twice as much per year as the years that follow.
According to LendingTree, families spend an estimated $29,325 annually during a child’s first five years, compared with roughly $12,000 per year during the remaining years through age 18.
Daycare is a major reason for the difference. Infant daycare costs approximately $17,000 annually across the U.S., while childcare expenses generally decline once children enter school.
Although the projected 18-year cost rose 1.9% to $303,418 nationwide, average annual expenses during the first five years fell 0.3% from the previous report, largely due to a slight decline in daycare costs.
The study’s estimates are based on a married, two-earner household with one child earning the national median family income. They primarily use 2024 cost data, and projected expenses are not adjusted for future inflation.
Childcare costs consume a larger share of earnings in the U.S. than the OECD average.
According to the OECD , childcare for a two-earner family with two young children cost approximately 20% of average earnings in the U.S., compared with 14% across OECD countries, based on 2021 data.
Countries such as Germany, Sweden, and Norway generally have lower out-of-pocket childcare costs, reflecting differences in government subsidies and public funding.
If you enjoyed this visualization, check out Mapped: What a Home Is Worth in Every U.S. State in 2026 on the Voronoi app.

Credit scores shape Americans’ abilities to get everything from credit cards to mortgages. This is bad news for Southerners.
A strong credit score can mean lower interest rates on mortgages, car loans, and credit cards, making it an important measure of Americans’ financial health.
But how does your state compare with the rest of the country?
This map shows average credit scores across all 50 states using Experian’s September 2025 data . Scores are based on FICO Score 8, which ranges from 300 to 850.
The Upper Midwest and New England dominate the top of the rankings, with Minnesota, Wisconsin, Vermont, and New Hampshire all averaging 735 or higher.
At the other end, several Southern states fall below 700, including Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, and South Carolina. The pattern highlights a clear geographic divide in average credit scores across the country.
The contrast extends to America’s largest state economies . Texas averages 692, well below California’s 721, while Florida’s 704 also falls short of the national average of 713.
The following table ranks U.S. states by their average credit scores as of September 2025.
Nationally, the average slipped from 715 in 2024 to 713 in 2025, marking a notable reversal after more than a decade of improving or stable scores.
Household budgets are also facing higher debt payments. Average monthly debt obligations reached $1,256 in 2025, up 2.6%, even as average total debt balances increased just 0.4%. Borrowers are paying more each month without taking on substantially larger balances.
One major change in 2025 was the return of negative reporting on federal student loans. After nearly five years of pandemic-era protections, missed payments began appearing on credit reports again, exposing struggling borrowers to sharp declines in their credit scores.

item.title: Can LLMs Supercharge Geolocations? Our Tests Show Big Improvements But Humans Remain Key

item.page_text:
Foeke is an investigator and trainer at Bellingcat. He has a background in conflict analysis and resolution and is particularly interested in military, environmental and human rights issues. Bluesky: @foeke.eurosky.social
Miguel is an Investigative Technologist for Bellingcat. He uses data and code to investigate and communicate stories, he experiments and builds research tools with and for the online investigations community.
Sign up here to receive Bellingcat’s biggest investigations by email as soon as they are published .
In September, the AI company Anthropic published a blog post that claimed its models were approaching “ superhuman capabilities for geolocating outdoor photos”. Anthropic made this claim by comparing its models’ performance to that of players of the popular online game GeoGuessr, which challenges users to geolocate Google Street View images.
Bellingcat has been running its own benchmark tests on AI models since June 2025, right around the time when Large Language Models (LLMs) began to challenge reverse image searches for assisting with geolocation tasks. In our first round, GPT 4o-mini from OpenAI appeared to be the best tool for geolocating, a title which was taken by Google AI mode when we performed our second round of tests a few months later in August 2025.
This time, we significantly upped the ante for the models, providing increasingly challenging photos and asking for only one set of coordinates. We tasked not only closed-weight models from Claude , Grok , Gemini , ChatGPT , and Mistral , but also open-weight models from Moonshot AI’s Kimi , commercial provider GeoSeer and the non-generative geolocation model GeoClip . In total, we fed each model 52 photos that had not been published anywhere on the internet before.
The results showed that the current generation of models have markedly improved geolocation capabilities. Anthropic’s Opus and Fable, as well as Google’s recent Gemini 4 Argon model, performed the best on geolocation tasks, narrowing down locations from images faster than a human could under specific conditions. Preliminary tests of a set of agentic skills and tools being developed internally by Bellingcat also showed promising results in further improving the geolocation performance of generic-use AI agents.
But crucially, the tests also showed why humans remain necessary for accurate and trustworthy geolocation work, as no models were foolproof. This is particularly important given the increased use of AI in military contexts. The Anthropic blog post focused specifically on geolocating photos for military and intelligence purposes such as targeting, a historically labour-intensive process requiring significant human expertise.
While our tests showed some models performed extremely well at narrowing down results to the correct general area, none were close to being perfect at finding the exact spot a picture was taken. That accuracy is extremely important in geolocation, especially in military contexts where the cost of incorrect information can be life or death . It is also important for organisations like Bellingcat whose reputation relies on pinpoint factual accuracy.
To compare model results, we used two metrics built on the distance in kilometres between a prediction and the real location. GeoGuessr Score was used to assess whether models could systematically identify the general area, while the Mean Log Score (explained below) measured which models most accurately pinpointed the correct location in the final few kilometres.
The GeoGuessr Score metric is based on the online game of the same name, whose scoring system Stanford University academics reverse-engineered in a 2024 study. This system rewards answers close to the general area an image was taken, but does not strongly distinguish between guesses close to the precise location. For example, an answer 200km from the correct location with more points than one 2,000km away. However, an answer 500m from where a picture was taken and another 5km away achieve a similar score. For real-world geolocations, that distance matters a great deal.
For more precision, we introduced a custom metric that grades models higher if they narrow down the search in the last few kilometres. This metric, the Mean Log Score, assigns a value from 0 (completely inaccurate) to 100 (perfect model) and works on a logarithmic scale instead of a linear one like GeoGuessr score.
Therefore, a 10-fold improvement in distance means the same whether it is from 5km to 500m or from 500km to 50km. You can compare both metrics here .
Below are the model results sorted by either metric, showing how many photos each model geolocated within distance bands from the true location.
Several models placed at least 10 out of the 52 photos correctly within one kilometre, and the top-performing models placed over 50 percent of the photos within 25 kilometres.
NOTE: Geoseer-fast refused to answer on four of the 52 photos, claiming “This image is not suitable for geolocation”, while Mistral-large-4 refused once with “insufficient information in image to identify location”. Kimi-k2.6 also failed to provide a set of coordinates on one photo, and Gemini 4 Argon timed out repeatedly on one photo.
To independently assess the models, we sought to give them very specific instructions and some images that were harder to geolocate than those provided in our past tests. The prompt asked for a single set of coordinates reflecting the photographer’s location. The purpose of restricting the response in this way was to prevent hedging, such as multiple guesses or confidence scores, and make the grading more uniform across different models. Models were allowed to use their providers’ built-in tools: search, code execution and page fetch. We capped their token output at 64,000 and ran each model under its default effort setting with a maximum time of 15 minutes per photo.
